description: Search-quality cases for Lögbrunnur, kept in Git so a ranking or provider change can be measured against the same inputs before it is merged. See docs/search-evaluation.md.

grades.3: the primary answer — the document the query is really asking for
grades.2: strongly relevant — a researcher would want it on the first page
grades.1: contextual — related and reasonable to return, not what was asked for

cases.note: A bare case number is a lookup, not a search. parseQuery flags it as isCaseNumberLookup; the case itself must be the top hit, not a judgment that happens to cite it.
The EFTA Court's lettered form. Exercises the same pattern through a different source and a different stored language.

Héraðsdómur numbers run to five digits. A pattern tuned to 2-4 digits drops them silently. topHitIsExact also guards the other direction: a trigram near-match on a different case number must never be served as the answer unmarked - see SearchHit.isFuzzy.

38/2001 is 'Lög um vexti og verðtryggingu' and is universally cited as 'vaxtalög' — a name its own title does not contain. This is what Act.aliases exists for; if it regresses, the most natural query for the act returns nothing.
Lög um meðferð einkamála. Cited by about a third of the corpus, so the act must outrank the judgments citing it.
A quoted phrase must be matched as a phrase. If the quotes are dropped the result set widens to every judgment containing either word, which is most of tort law.
þ/ð/æ/ö survive tokenisation. A character class that quietly drops them empties the query rather than failing.
NOT becomes websearch's -negation. Verified by the excluded term being absent, not by a count.
A broad topical query. Nothing to label a single right answer for; it is here so a change that empties a common query is caught.
For immigration the case law is at the board, not the courts. Also checks that source scoping actually scopes.
The strict opt-in promise: a ticked source is the only source that answers.
The journals are searched alongside the case law but are not decisions; a query scoped to them must return only articles.
JCDs are stored in English. Their own heading is the only description they carry.
The other direction: a fuzzy fallback tuned too loosely returns plausible-looking rubbish for a query that should be empty. In a legal tool that is worse than nothing.

Judgments award 'dráttarvaxta' and 'dráttarvöxtum'; almost none write the nominative plural the query uses. The stem itself changes (vextir/vaxta/vöxtum), so no prefix, substring or trigram match reaches them either — this is only findable through the lemma. Before prisma/sql/setup-lemmas.sql, the most natural query for the commonest money claim in the corpus missed most of it.

The act is cited as 'stjórnsýslulögum' or 'stjórnsýslulaga' and essentially never in the nominative. Note that the ö/a shift makes 'stjórnsýslulaga' unreachable by prefix, while 'stjórnsýslulögum' is a superset of the query string — which is exactly why someHitLacksWord matches whole words and not substrings.
Employment cases are argued in the genitive — 'lögmæti uppsagnar', 'vegna uppsagnarinnar'. ö→a again, so the inflected forms share only a prefix with the query.

The hardest of these, and the one that shows why a hand-built synonym list would not have done. BÍN lemmatises 'skaðabætur' to the SINGULAR 'skaðabót', so the query a lawyer would actually type is not the lemma — it is mapped to one, and from there reaches 'skaðabóta' and 'skaðabótum'. Nothing about that is guessable from the query string.

Purely suffixal: 'gæsluvarðhaldi', 'gæsluvarðhalds'. Held out because it is the easy shape of the problem — the one a naive prefix match would appear to solve — and it is worth knowing whether a change fixes the easy case while breaking the stem-changing ones above.

Appears in nearly every judgment in the corpus, and nearly always as 'málskostnaðar' or 'málskostnaði' in the operative sentence. A high-frequency term is the case most likely to expose lemma matching going too wide, which is what the recall floor here is really watching.

The guard on the other side. A quoted phrase is deliberately never lemmatised — adjacency in the lemma vector is only approximate, and someone who quotes a phrase is asking for those words. This must keep behaving exactly as it did before setup-lemmas.sql existed: every hit contains the phrase, as written.
